text:
Madame de Nevers and Madame de Martigues, on leaving her house, went to the Dauphin Queen’s apartments; Monsieur de Clèves was there. This princess asked them where they had come from; they told her that they had come from Monsieur de Clèves’s house, where they had spent part of the afternoon with a great many people, and that they had left only Monsieur de Nemours there. These words, which they thought so inconsequential, were not so to Monsieur de Clèves. Although he must well have imagined that Monsieur de Nemours could often find opportunities to speak to his wife, nevertheless the thought that he was at her house, that he was there alone, and that he could speak to her of his love, appeared to him at that moment so novel and so unbearable that jealousy flared up in his heart with greater violence than it had ever done before. It was impossible for him to remain with the Queen; he returned home, not even knowing why he was returning or whether he intended to go and interrupt Monsieur de Nemours. As soon as he drew near his house, he looked to see whether he could discern anything that might enable him to judge whether that prince was still there: he felt relief on seeing that he was no longer there, and found comfort in thinking that he could not have remained there long. He imagined that perhaps it was not Monsieur de Nemours of whom he ought to be jealous; and although he had no doubt of it, he sought to doubt it; but so many things would have convinced him of it that he did not remain long in the uncertainty he desired. He went at once to his wife’s chamber, and after speaking to her for some time about indifferent matters, he could not keep himself from asking her what she had done and whom she had seen; she gave him an account of it. When he saw that she did not name Monsieur de Nemours, he asked her, trembling, whether that was everyone she had seen, in order to give her an opportunity to name that prince and to avoid the pain of having her dissemble the matter with him. Since she had not seen him, she did not name him; and Monsieur de Clèves resumed, in a tone that revealed his distress:

“And Monsieur de Nemours,” he said to her, “did you not see him, or have you forgotten him?”

“I did not see him, in fact,” she replied; “I was feeling unwell, and I sent one of my women to make my apologies to him.”

“Then you were feeling unwell only for him,” Monsieur de Clèves replied. “Since you saw everyone else, why make distinctions for Monsieur de Nemours? Why is he not like any other man to you? Why must you fear the sight of him? Why do you let him see that you fear it? Why do you make him aware that you are making use of the power his passion gives you over him? Would you dare refuse to see him if you did not know full well that he distinguishes your severity from discourtesy? But why must you show severity toward him? From a person such as you, Madame, everything except indifference is a favor.”

“I did not think,” Madame de Clèves replied, “whatever suspicions you may have concerning Monsieur de Nemours, that you could reproach me for not having seen him.”

“Yet I do reproach you for it, Madame,” he answered, “and my reproaches are well founded. Why not see him if he has said nothing to you? But, Madame, he has spoken to you; if his silence alone had revealed his passion to you, it would not have made so great an impression upon you. You could not tell me the whole truth; you concealed the greater part of it from me; you even repented of the little you confessed to me, and you did not have the strength to continue. I am more unhappy than I believed, and I am the unhappiest of all men. You are my wife, I love you as my mistress, and I see you love another. That other man is the most lovable man at court, and he sees you every day; he knows that you love him. Ah! I was able to believe,” he cried, “that you would overcome the passion you have for him. I must have lost my reason to have believed it possible.”

“I do not know,” Madame de Clèves replied sadly, “whether you were wrong to judge so favorably of conduct as extraordinary as mine; but I do not know whether I was not mistaken in believing that you would do me justice.”

“Do not doubt it, Madame,” Monsieur de Clèves replied, “you were mistaken; you expected from me things as impossible as those I expected from you. How could you hope that I would retain my reason? Had you then forgotten that I loved you desperately and that I was your husband? Either one of the two can drive a man to extremes: what can the two together not do? Ah! And what are they not doing!” he continued. “I have nothing but violent and uncertain feelings over which I have no control. I no longer find myself worthy of you; you no longer appear worthy of me. I adore you, I hate you; I offend you, I ask your forgiveness; I admire you, I am ashamed to admire you. In short, there is no longer either calm or reason in me. I do not know how I have been able to live since you spoke to me at Coulommiers, and since the day you learned from Madame the Dauphin that your affair was known. I cannot unravel how it came to be known, or what passed between Monsieur de Nemours and you on that subject: you will never explain it to me, and I do not ask you to explain it to me. I ask you only to remember that you have made me the unhappiest man in the world.”

Monsieur de Clèves left his wife after these words and departed the following day without seeing her; but he wrote her a letter full of sorrow, honor, and tenderness. She made so moving a reply, so filled with assurances concerning both her past conduct and the conduct she would maintain in the future, that, as her assurances were founded on truth and these were indeed her feelings, the letter made an impression on Monsieur de Clèves and gave him some peace; added to which, since Monsieur de Nemours was going to join the King just as he was, he had the comfort of knowing that Monsieur de Nemours would not be in the same place as Madame de Clèves. Whenever this princess spoke to her husband, the passion he showed her, the honorable nature of his conduct, the affection she had for him, and what she owed him made impressions upon her heart that weakened the image of Monsieur de Nemours; but this was only for a time, and that image soon returned, more vivid and more present than before.

During the first days after that prince’s departure, she scarcely felt his absence; afterward it seemed cruel to her. Since she had loved him, not a day had passed on which she had not feared or hoped to encounter him, and she found it very painful to think that it was no longer within the power of chance to cause her to meet him.

She went to Coulommiers; and before going there, she took care to have brought there some large paintings she had had copied from originals that Madame de Valentinois had commissioned for her beautiful house at Anet. All the notable events that had occurred during the King’s reign were depicted in these paintings. Among them was the siege of Metz, and all those who had distinguished themselves there were painted with a strong likeness. Monsieur de Nemours was among them, and this was perhaps what had made Madame de Clèves wish to possess these paintings.

Madame de Martigues, who had been unable to depart with the court, promised to spend a few days with her at Coulommiers. The Queen’s favor, which they shared, had caused neither envy nor estrangement between them; they were friends, though without confiding their feelings to one another. Madame de Clèves knew that Madame de Martigues loved the Vidame; but Madame de Martigues did not know that Madame de Clèves loved Monsieur de Nemours, nor that she was loved by him. Madame de Clèves’s status as the Vidame’s niece made her dearer to Madame de Martigues; and Madame de Clèves also loved her as a person who, like herself, was in love, and whose passion was for her lover’s intimate friend.
